extracted.intended_audience: political scientists, students of public opinion and journalism, and informed readers interested in democracy and the press
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of newspapers and public opinion
extracted.subtask_description: Critical exposition of democratic representation (guild/social functional democracy) and the role of newspapers in forming public opinion; assesses institutional requirements, limits of self-government, and economic/organizational constraints on the press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism must express men's social wills
rubrics_metrics.description: The object is "to get the mechanism right, and to adjust it as far as possible to the expression of men's social wills."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion demands institutional arrangements that enable self-expression in self-government "in any and every form of social action." It underlies the guildsmen's aim but the author warns that getting the mechanism right is difficult because of complexity, external relations, and limits of direct knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factory/shop as the democratic unit
rubrics_metrics.description: The factory (taken loosely to include mines, ship-stations, yards, docks — 'a natural center of production') is 'the natural and fundamental unit of industrial democracy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The shop is a workplace small enough for direct personal contact so that 'every individual member of the Guild' can exercise self-government. But the text warns that the shop is distinct from an industry and that larger interests (wages, marketing, planning) are not purely internal to the shop, creating serious limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-government limited to internal shop affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-government in the purely internal affairs of the shop is feasible because such affairs 'can be taken in at a single view.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion recognizes the shop can handle personnel temperament, petty industrial justice, and act as a unit with other shops, but stresses isolation is impossible and many big issues (wages, standards, marketing) are external and require broader coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative government arranged federatively from shop to nation
rubrics_metrics.description: Management of external relations requires representative government 'arranged in a federal order from the shop to the plant, the plant to the industry, the industry to the nation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because representatives originate from self-governing units, the federal organism will theoretically be inspired by self-government. The author warns practical risks: perpetual logrolling or chaotic conflict among shops when representatives must decide on matters beyond shop experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional representation (representatives for functions, not groups)
rubrics_metrics.description: The only representative possible is one who acts for 'some particular function,' so each person must help choose as many representatives 'as there are distinct essential groups of functions to be performed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this rubric representatives speak for functions rather than groups. It implies multiple functional votes per person. The author notes problems: defining functions, voting frequency, and the uninstructed voter problem (who 'waives his right to vote' or can be manipulated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Voters must have direct experience of the interest they represent
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional democracy presumes 'men vote candidly according to their own interests, which it is assumed they know by daily experience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This works inside self-contained groups, but fails for external relations where groups lack direct experience. Hence representatives must stretch beyond direct experience or public opinion will be a product of education/propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinions about industry and society require education/propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: The public opinions of a shop about its rights and duties in the industry and in society are matters of education or propaganda, not the automatic product of shop-consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because shops cannot spontaneously reach valid views about the whole industry or nation, forming public opinion on such matters requires deliberate teaching, information assembly, and persuasion; otherwise representatives generalize wrongly from narrow experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions must be clearly defined and accepted for functional democracy to work
rubrics_metrics.description: Guild socialists imagine society analyzed into functions which are 'in turn synthesized harmoniously' and that there will be 'essential agreement about the purposes of society as a whole' and about the role of every organized group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats the problem of recognizing 'distinct essential groups of functions' as acute: who defines functions (trade unions, communes, or other bodies)? If the state defines functions, the premise of voluntary functional relations collapses; vested interests and hardened group identities may persist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy should be judged by processes and results, not only origin of power
rubrics_metrics.description: The democratic fallacy is preoccupation with the origin of government rather than with the processes and results; criteria should include whether government produces standards of living that realize human dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate government by objective outputs—health, decent housing, material necessities, education, freedom, pleasures, beauty—rather than only by whether it 'expresses the will of the people.' This shifts emphasis from mere self-government to measurable human welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Devise standards of living and audits to control public officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Social control depends upon devising standards of living and methods of audit by which the acts of public officials and industrial directors are measured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because citizens cannot directly guide all acts, progressively increasing control requires that acts be plainly recorded and their results objectively measured. The working out of such standards and audits has only begun.

rubrics_metrics.name: The press must make the invisible environment visible to citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a political problem of 'how to make the invisible world visible to the citizens of a modern state' and the press/newsgathering machinery are central to that task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political science historically neglected news-gathering. Assembling information about complex/distant matters is technical and expensive; the press must provide reliable reporting so citizens can form informed opinions for governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain civil liberties/free speech as necessary (but not sufficient) for truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil liberties and freedom of speech are of immense practical value: 'Who ever knew Truth put to the worse, in a free and open encounter?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Free discussion helps truth emerge over time and prevents suppression damage. However, for complex/invisible matters free speech alone is insufficient because truth about distant/technical issues requires organized information-gathering, not merely open debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspapers are commercial enterprises: circulation is a means to an end
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulation is the means to an end; the newspaper editor 'has to be re-elected every day.' The newspaper is compared to a business whose circulation attracts advertisers who pay for access to consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial decisions are constrained by the need to attract and retain paying readers and advertisers. Types of circulation (quality vs mass) are judged by what advertisers want; newspapers must balance content to serve both readership and advertising revenue streams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readers pay indirectly for news and expect low prices; advertising funds journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader will pay a nominal price and pay indirectly through other purchases; 'the citizen will pay for his telephone, his railroad rides... he will however, pay handsomely for the privilege of having someone read about him.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because readers resist paying the full cost openly, advertising subsidizes news. This economic reality shapes what newspapers provide: entertainment, inexpensive packaging, and content attractive to advertisers rather than purely civic information.

rubrics_metrics.name: A newspaper that angers its paying customers/advertisers is a bad newspaper
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper which angers those whom it pays is a bad newspaper; 'it would be regarded as an outrage to have to pay openly the price of a good ice cream soda for all the news of the world.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial independence is constrained by commercial relationships: alienating advertisers or the audience undermines viability. The press cannot be equated morally/economically with endowed institutions (schools, churches) or disinterested professions in the way its financing and responsibilities function.
